figures.article_title: A policy beside the prompt: a proposal that every agent takes a behaviour policy as an input, with enforcement and liability attached, and why aviation and payments say the vendors should want it

figures.article_title: If somebody built a company on code review: how I would do it, and why it is only now possible
figures.alt: What is fractal and what is not. The constant across every codebase is the grammar: nodes, edges, an ontology, a taxonomy and a way to zoom in and out. Which layers exist, what they are called, which languages fill the bottom layers and what the business counts as a change that matters are decided by the company you are in. The first article's seven altitudes were one Python repository's layers, not the layers.

figures.article_title: If somebody built a company on code review: how I would do it, and why it is only now possible
figures.alt: Two graphs, one grammar. The projected graph is built top down before the code exists: objectives, stories with their rules and examples, features and flows, the commands and surfaces they will touch, and the components as far as design can see. The derived graph is built bottom up from the syntax tree. The review is the join, and the join has three outcomes.

figures.article_title: If somebody built a company on code review: how I would do it, and why it is only now possible
figures.alt: Three changes, three held layers. Tidying a method holds the class shapes and is proved by unit tests on them. Migrating an architecture holds the client interface and is proved by contract tests on it, while everything below is new. A change that holds nothing is not a refactor, whatever the commit message says, and the review should treat it as a fix or a feature.

figures.article_title: If somebody built a company on code review: how I would do it, and why it is only now possible
figures.alt: Code review by stage of evolution. For explorer code, review is for speed and feedback and the person reads the behaviour, not the lines. For villager code it is for quality and reachability, all the way down, because this is where changes land. For town planner code it is for guarantees at the boundary, read by deterministic checks with a person for the exceptions. The company sits in the two moves between columns.

figures.article_title: If somebody built a company on code review: how I would do it, and why it is only now possible
figures.alt: Reshape the change before you review it. A pull request as it arrived, and the same change split by what it can reach: the part that provably reaches no behaviour, the part that reaches behaviour through tested paths, and the part that reaches a mission-critical path or a layer with no test holding it. Review is sorting what can go fast from what must go slow. Counts are illustrative.

figures.article_title: If somebody built a company on code review: how I would do it, and why it is only now possible
figures.alt: Two mechanisms. Left, a budget per altitude and per change, decided in advance: deterministic checks always run and cost compute, the delta re-derives only what the change touched, a model summarising has a small budget and a hard stop, a model proposing has a larger one and every output marked proposed, onboarding is budgeted per slice, and work handed from agent to agent carries its budget with it. Right, the five whys as the loop: a bug at one layer is a question about the layer below, and the fix is a rule there, so the next change like it is caught for the price of a query. Budgets are illustrative.

figures.article_title: No server, by design: first I retired the database, now I am retiring the back end

figures.article_title: No server, by design: first I retired the database, now I am retiring the back end

figures.article_title: The SaaS apocalypse will be decided by inertia, not by AI
figures.alt: The incumbent and the newcomer are carrying the same AI. What differs is the ball and chain of past success, and the fact that the newcomer was never on the rails in the first place.

figures.article_title: The SaaS apocalypse will be decided by inertia, not by AI
figures.alt: The SaaS product slides right along the evolution axis and becomes a substrate: a database, a message bus, a state machine. On top of that substrate, the custom brief is now cheap to make. What is not cheap is making it last, and that is the handover from explorer to villager to town planner. The mistake, drawn in red, is treating the brief as if it were already a product.

figures.article_title: Sell, don't issue: a funding model for founders who have already won, where the investor buys the founder's shares, the founder lends the company what it needs, and open source keeps everyone honest
figures.alt: The two-part model: the investor buys the founder's ordinary shares and pays the founder; the founder lends part of the proceeds to the company as a subordinated loan; the company gets cash without new shares; and the investor's protection is the open-source fork, not a board seat.

figures.article_title: Sell, don't issue: a funding model for founders who have already won, where the investor buys the founder's shares, the founder lends the company what it needs, and open source keeps everyone honest
figures.alt: The same £2 million, two ways, for a UK company worth £10 million: the founder keeps 80% either way; a standard round gives the investor new preferred shares, rights and control, and puts £2 million into the company; selling and lending gives the investor ordinary shares and the fork as protection, and leaves the founder about £1.58 million after tax, to lend back as much as the company needs; and bought shares carry no EIS relief.
figures.description: Table infographic 'The same £2 million, two ways': rows (founder's stake, what the investor gets, rights, protection, cash into company, founder's cash after tax, investor's UK tax relief) compared across grey 'Standard round' and teal 'Sell and lend' columns; one red cell 'None: bought shares do not qualify'.

figures.article_title: Send an agent, not a spreadsheet: the next generation of software due diligence, and why the companies that stopped reading their code are about to be asked about it
figures.alt: Due diligence as it was and as it can be. The questionnaire measures whether the vendor has a document with the right title, is written by the vendor and connects to nothing. The agent reads what is there, under a behaviour policy, inside the vendor's environment, and the vendor reviews what leaves. The difference is not who controls the answer. It is that the thing being described can no longer be described into shape.

figures.article_title: Send an agent, not a spreadsheet: the next generation of software due diligence, and why the companies that stopped reading their code are about to be asked about it
figures.alt: Six questions a due diligence agent asks. Each has a good answer, an acceptable answer for the product's risk level, and a silence, and the agent does not need the vendor to say which; it can see. The table is illustrative, the shape is not.

figures.article_title: Send an agent, not a spreadsheet: the next generation of software due diligence, and why the companies that stopped reading their code are about to be asked about it
figures.alt: The same questions, a different bar for each kind of product. A prototype passes by saying what it is and mapping what it can reach. A product with customers needs review or tests on every path a customer depends on. A product holding other people's data needs behaviour policies for its agents and a record of what shipped unreviewed. Mission-critical software needs checks at the boundary the buyer can rerun. Honesty about the tier is the first answer.

figures.article_title: Send an agent, not a spreadsheet: the next generation of software due diligence, and why the companies that stopped reading their code are about to be asked about it
figures.alt: An agent behaviour policy read as a due diligence document. The left is a deploy agent's policy for a fictional vendor. The right is what a buyer reads off it: the worst case, which lines are enforced by the identity and which are only instructions, which risks the vendor has accepted on the buyer's behalf, and what it means when a vendor with agents in the pipeline has no policy to show.

figures.article_title: Send an agent, not a spreadsheet: the next generation of software due diligence, and why the companies that stopped reading their code are about to be asked about it
figures.alt: Who the agent finds, and who gets ahead. The company that stopped reading has nothing to show. The incumbent that never understood its own software has a questionnaire answer for everything and a graph for nothing. The startup that doubles down has less code and the same tools, and can answer before it is asked.

figures.article_title: The controllable founder: why investors pick one founder over another who looks just as good, and what record labels taught us about who the commodity is
figures.alt: We study the survivors: of everyone who made the same moves, a few won and are studied; others were funded, did the same and failed; most did the same and were never funded. A risky practice can be unrelated to success across everyone and still look like its cause among survivors. Illustrative.

figures.article_title: The controllable founder: why investors pick one founder over another who looks just as good, and what record labels taught us about who the commodity is
figures.alt: Who is the commodity: in music, the songs, the producers, the venues and radio stay scarce while the performer is moved towards commodity; in venture, the investor's network stays scarce while the founder is moved the same way. A sketch of the argument, not a measured map.

figures.article_title: The controllable founder: why investors pick one founder over another who looks just as good, and what record labels taught us about who the commodity is
figures.alt: Control moves with performance: when a company performs poorly, investors take full control; as it improves, the founder gains control; when it performs very well, investors keep their cash-flow rights but give up most control. A schematic of Kaplan and Strömberg's finding, not their data.

figures.article_title: The expert founders: why the next startups will be built by the people who know the problem, and why Europe's slower, sceptical money suits them

figures.description: Two vertical five-step flows 'Two playbooks: the outsider with capital, and the expert with agents': left (grey/orange/blue/red) Find a gap, Raise first, Hire the experts, Execute and displace, Become the incumbent; right (teal/blue/orange/purple) Live the problem, Build it with agents, Show it working, Raise for scale not discovery, Stay close to the field.

The founders can leave if no broad non-compete stops them; the investors can fund a team next door if they can pay for it; the customers can move if their data leaves with them, cheaply. Illustrative.

figures.article_title: The man behind the curtain: the emails from my agents are from me, there is an article behind each one, and every line has to buy the next
figures.alt: In front of the curtain, what the person receiving the email sees: one email, in my name. Behind it, two things. The agents: they draft the reply, follow up the thread, map what was said in a CRM, collect the evidence and keep track of what is owed. And me: I read every draft, use it to think, change it, often ask for an article so the answer has evidence behind it, and then send it. The agents send nothing.

figures.article_title: The man behind the curtain: the emails from my agents are from me, there is an article behind each one, and every line has to buy the next
figures.alt: One article, many emails. On the left, emails arriving with questions, a few hundred words each. In the middle, the test: is there an article that answers this? If yes, the reply is short and links it. If no, the agents write one and check it against its sources, it is published, I read it, and the reply links it. On the right, the article: written once, linked from every later reply, read later, forwarded, corrected as new versions.

figures.article_title: The man behind the curtain: the emails from my agents are from me, there is an article behind each one, and every line has to buy the next
figures.alt: Every part of an email buys the next. The subject buys the first line, which buys the first paragraph, which buys the email, which buys the article. Below, the same first email two ways: starting with a banner, where the inbox preview shows the banner's text; and starting with a plain paragraph that answers the question, where the preview is the answer.

figures.article_title: For a startup, the most important question is whether they miss it
figures.alt: The loop. Ship something usable, give it away briefly, take it away, and find out whether anybody misses it. A no sends you back to the start with better information. A yes is the only thing that earns the right to charge, and charging at a profit is the only thing that earns the right to choose your investors.

figures.article_title: For a startup, the most important question is whether they miss it
figures.alt: The startup test. Ship it, let them try it, take it away, and see whether anybody asks for it back.

Take it away.' over a photoreal desk scene (plant, mug 'Good Work Today', notebook 'Plan/Build/Ship', app-icon tiles with one lifted by a hand and an orange speech bubble 'Can I have it back?', books 'Customers/Revenue/Freedom'); bottom strip 01 Build for profit, 02 Raise from strength, 03 Open source everything, 'sgit.ai'.

figures.article_title: The value of constraints: what client-side encryption and open source actually gave us, which is not what you would think
figures.alt: Two constraints and what they take away: client-side encryption forbids the server from reading the data and removes the temptation to process there; open source, all of it, forbids private code and removes lock-in, the evaluation edition and building every customer's integration.

figures.article_title: The value of constraints: what client-side encryption and open source actually gave us, which is not what you would think
figures.alt: Encryption on the client moves the problem from the data to the keys: a server that can read has to protect all the data, runs code next to it, and puts the sovereignty line where the data is; a server that holds ciphertext needs the keys protected, runs no code next to the data, and puts the line at whoever holds the keys.

figures.article_title: Two years in, the opposite: an essay about burning out on AI that I could not buy, and why my two years of AI have been the most productive of my career
figures.alt: One visit, two models. On the left, what the visit to the essay gave: the headline, the byline, three paragraphs and adverts in three places, then a box offering a 14-day trial that renews at $12.95 every four weeks, or $49 for a year that renews at $149. On the right, what Dinis wanted: read the essay, pay a few pence for what he read, a share to the author, the option to challenge it or say the headline was unfair, and trust earned over many articles before any subscription.

figures.article_title: What can your agent reach? RiskMandate and the Agent Behaviour Policy, explained for the person who has to decide
figures.alt: One agent, three sets. The grant is everything the agent can actually reach through its credentials and connectors; the mandate is what the organisation authorised it to do; the delta is the difference, the authority nobody accepted. Each capability in the grant carries a barrier: nothing in the way, a rule in prose, a setting the agent's own account can change, or a boundary enforced above it. Only the last bounds anything.

figures.article_title: What can your agent reach? RiskMandate and the Agent Behaviour Policy, explained for the person who has to decide
figures.alt: Five ways into the room, each a question someone already has to answer: a contract, where legal and procurement ask what the vendor's agent will do with the data; a security questionnaire, where a customer asks which agents touch their data; an insurance renewal, where the question is whether AI is excluded from cover; the board's risk appetite, where the question is who can pull the plug; and twenty minutes, where anyone running an assistant asks what it can actually do.

figures.description: Two vertical five-step flows 'Two playbooks: the outsider with capital, and the expert with agents': left (grey/orange/blue/red) Find a gap, Raise first, Hire the experts, Execute and displace, Become the incumbent; right (teal/blue/orange/purple) Live the problem, Build it with agents, Show it working, Raise for scale not discovery, Stay close to the field.

figures.article_title: Your own newsroom: how a founder can tell their story by voice memo, with an agent that checks it and publishes it to GitHub Pages, and readers who pay a little if they find it useful
figures.alt: The loop: speak a memo; an agent session connected to one repository researches, writes and checks it; it commits and pushes; GitHub Actions validates and publishes to GitHub Pages; readers read, rate and top up through a payment link you own; and the record grows.
